E1256.summary: Christ, cited in the Appendix (Table Talk) for sayings Atwood applies to the Hermetic Art and the Stone.
E1256.body: Cited only in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). His words “The wind bloweth where it listeth” are cited as an analogy, Christ the Head Corner Stone is named as the analogue of the Stone, and the regenerated are said to enter his life [APP ¶41, APP ¶46, APP ¶60]. His saying “Seek ye first the Kingdom of God and His righteousness and all these things shall be added unto you” supports Atwood's point that seeking the Universal first is the shortest and truest road in the Hermetic Art [APP ¶134]. His use of the language of David — “I have said ye are gods, if (says our Lord) ye called them gods unto whom the Word of God came” — illustrates powers subordinate to God evolved where the Word comes, with the danger of self-centers [APP ¶100].

E1257.summary: Unnamed metaphysicians whom Atwood sets in contrast: they lamented natural reason's inadequacy but could not free it from dependence on sense.
E1257.body: Atwood cites them by way of contrast: they lamented the inadequacy of natural reason but could not free it from its dependence on sense [II.1 ¶32].

E1258.summary: An unnamed modern writer whom Atwood cites to confirm and illustrate Hermes' process in terms of the three principles.
E1258.body: Atwood cites this unnamed modern exponent as confirming and illustrating Hermes' process in terms of the three principles: “in three months circulation, says he, by digestion, the powder becomes black” [II.1 ¶23].

E1259.summary: Cosmopolite's allegorical name for the Mercury, as reported by Eudoxus; apt because the Mercury is the first matter of all metals.
E1259.body: Voice: Eudoxus (quoted). He explains that Cosmopolite's allegory — “give our old man gold and silver to swallow” — names the Mercury: “Our Old Man is our Mercury” [IV.3 ¶10]. The name fits, he says, because the Mercury is the first matter of all metals [IV.3 ¶10].

E1260.summary: Eudoxus' name for the matter leavened by the Perfect Body, with the Spirit uniting them, compounded in proportions learned from bread-making.
E1260.body: Voice: Eudoxus (quoted). The paste is the matter leavened by the Perfect Body, the Spirit uniting them; it is composed of several matters whose proportions are learned from the analogy of bread-making — “the matters which compose our philosophical paste” [IV.3 ¶14]. Once fermented, all the philosophic confection becomes itself a leaven [IV.3 ¶14].

E1261.summary: Sendivogius' term for the philosophers' own gold and silver, called living, as opposed to common gold and silver, called dead.
E1261.body: Voice: Sendivogius (quoted). The philosophers' own gold and silver are called living, against common gold and silver, called dead: “take Ours which are living” [IV.3 ¶21]. The text does not positively define them here.

E1262.summary: Poet whom Atwood calls an initiated poet and quotes from the Fasti and Metamorphoses on Chaos, the Aether, man's origin and the steep first way.
E1262.body: Atwood presents him as an initiated poet, inspired, “as he declares, by that same universal deity of the two-faced Janus” [III.3 ¶44]. From the Fasti she quotes “Me Chaos antiqui, nam res sum prisca, vocabant.” — Chaos as the primeval thing, opening the cosmogony [III.3 ¶45, III.3 n30]. From the Metamorphoses: “Ille opifex rerum, mundi melioris origo”, illustrating man made from divine seed or from earth holding seeds of heaven [III.3 ¶46, III.3 ¶47, III.3 n31]; “Haec super imposuit liquidam et gravitate carentem, Aethera”, placing the dreg-free Aether above the rest and introducing the Etheral Quintessence [III.2 ¶37, III.2 n33]; and “Ardua prima via est”, the steepness of the first way [IV.1 ¶8, IV.1 n11]. (Renderings of the Latin are readers' own, not the book's.) Elsewhere he is named with Virgil, Horace and Vitruvius among Augustan men accused of sorcery, illustrating Rome's limited achievement [I.1 ¶18].

E1263.summary: The one universal Nature: in the Orphic hymn the whole that is all elements; for Atwood the Alchemical Pan, one in himself and multitudinous in offspring.
E1263.body: In the Orphic hymn Atwood quotes, Pan is “Fortis subtilis Pan, integer et generalis; Et totus ignis, aura, terra, sive aqua,” — the beginning and end of all [I.2 ¶28]. Atwood then turns to “the most Ancient Nature”, speaking of it as he: “Yet not in his elementary immanifest diffusion let us invoke the most Ancient Nature”, but as the Hermetic masters found it [I.2 ¶29]. In her own voice the subject is a single being with manifold offspring: “so is it said to be with the Alchemical Pan, who, being but one himself, is in his offspring multitudinous” [I.2 ¶34]; he contains Proteus and evolves all forms from his central will [I.2 ¶34].

E1264.summary: What the purged, pure life flows forth as, in a declaration Atwood reports.
E1264.body: In an unattributed declaration (“as is declared”), the purged pure life flows forth as “a pure panacea from the god of Light” [III.1 ¶10].

E1265.summary: Writer Atwood cites as describing several perpetual lamps.
E1265.body: Cited as describing several perpetual lamps [I.1 ¶18, I.1 ¶20].

E1266.summary: A figure in Democritus' image who appears golden under the fire and is then called such a Venus.
E1266.body: Voice: Democritus (quoted). In his image Paphia, under the fire, appears golden, and is then identified with Venus: “Perchance, it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus” [I.3 n53].

E1267.summary: A group named in a chapter title, cited for the view that the true medicine and fire of life are bound in man.
E1267.body: Named in the chapter title. Atwood cites them in support of the view that the medicine and fire of life (called Antimony) are in man and are freed by purgation: “The true medicine, according to the Paracelsians, is bound in man” [III.1 ¶1, III.1 ¶10].

E1268.summary: Authority Atwood cites often, chiefly on Separation as the Art's primary object and on the tincture, while criticizing his deliberately misleading writings.
E1268.body:
Atwood calls him “our doctor” and draws on him chiefly for Separation. From the addresses To the Athenians: “The greatest miracle of all in philosophy is separation”, with the true element as the spirit of life and First Matter of the elements [I.2 ¶25, I.2 ¶26, I.2 n21, I.2 n24]; and “Separation is the greatest miracle in philosophy”, the Art's primary object, with free will as friend or foe and the sequestatrix [III.1 ¶21, III.1 n20]. In the Signatura Rerum he describes the tincture's astral fire, signs, and transmuting and medicinal power: “Our tincture of gold” [I.1 ¶76, I.1 n99]. He supports whiteness as the simple ground of diversity whereon to recreate: “Omnia in Dei manu alba sunt; is eas tingit ut vult” [III.2 ¶5]; and he is said to agree concerning the Matter [III.2 ¶60]. With Van Helmont he corroborates the appearance of the Universal Idea — “by separation of their parts the specific impress is to be perceived in the vessel containing the decomposed spirit” — though Atwood qualifies this as only a secondary witness [III.3 n27].

She also criticizes him for deliberately misleading writings, names his best works (the three Addresses to the Athenians, Aurora) and discusses his death [I.1 ¶64]. Cited with his Libro de Vita longa, he is compared to Avicenna's ill-directed genius and appears to credit Artephius's tale [I.1 ¶35, I.1 ¶36, I.1 n41]. His De Natura Rerum was published with French's New Light, 1650 [I.1 ¶71]. He is mentioned as calling Crollius a natural divine, with “salem Paracelsi” in the Latin [II.1 ¶14, II.1 ¶21].

In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer): “the Archaeus of Paracelsus” is set in apposition to the solar plexus, workshop of the Celestial life [APP ¶32]; he is the source of “evestrum” for the soul's destiny-dream [APP ¶57] and of the name Evester for the analogical sphere [APP ¶105]; and mesmerism is said to imitate the Divine Art of separation he speaks of [APP ¶73].

E1269.summary: Followers of Paracelsus who, Atwood says, applied alchemy to human life and suggested the method and medium of attraction.
E1269.body: Cited as having applied alchemy to human life and suggested “the method and medium of attraction” [II.1 ¶9].

E1270.summary: Work (author not named in the text) quoted to illustrate Mammon as the downward-looking spirit leading the depraved operators.
E1270.body: Atwood quotes it on Mammon, the downward-looking spirit who leads the depraved operators: “for e’en in heaven his looks and thoughts Were always downward bent” [III.4 ¶4, III.4 ¶5, III.4 n2]. The author is not named.

E1271.summary: Paris, who preferred Venus to Juno and Minerva, invoked to illustrate the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) in the Democritus passage.
E1271.body: Invoked to illustrate the beauty of the golden Venus (Paphia) of the Democritus passage: “Perchance it was when Paris gazed on such a Venus, he did prefer her both to Juno and Minerva” [IV.1 ¶43]. Whether Atwood or the quoted source speaks here is unclear.

E1272.summary: Authority whose Non-Being Atwood identifies with the Matter, cited on non-being and the initial nonentity of all.
E1272.body: Atwood quotes his Fragments on “Non-being, which nor mind can see”, as a check on intellectual notions along this path [III.2 ¶13, III.2 ¶14, III.2 n14]. Via Aristotle she reports that he touched the One according to Reason and saw more than Xenophanes and Melissus [III.2 ¶40]. He is cited with the rest to prove the initial nonentity of all [III.2 ¶54], and “the Non-Being of Parmenides” is identified with the Matter [III.2 ¶60].

E1273.summary: Vaughan's term for an individual spirit that a certain Art unites to the Universal; distinguished from the divine spirit.
E1273.body: Voice: Vaughan (quoted): “a certain Art by which a Particular Spirit may be united to the Universal” [II.1 ¶26]. The Particular Spirit is distinguished from the divine spirit [II.1 ¶26].

E1274.summary: The Spirit made passive, into which the supernatural reason infuses itself throughout.
E1274.body: Atwood: the supernatural reason works “by pure infusion of Itself to the passified Spirit throughout” [III.1 ¶21].

E1275.summary: Aristotle's term, as Atwood reports and adopts it, for an intellect capable of receiving and being converted to all things.
E1275.body: Aristotle's term as Atwood reports it (and adopts): the intellect he “calls passive intellect, because capable of receiving and being converted to all” [II.2 ¶17].

E1276.summary: The receptive intelligence, identified with the Moon, which, freed by art and in conjunction, answers the Will of her seeking Reason.
E1276.body: Atwood: the Passive Intelligence, spoken of as her, once freed by art and set in conjunction, “responds to the Will of her seeking Reason”, finds the way, removes obstacles and passes with him through the abyss [III.1 ¶40]. Identity asserted: “the Moon is singularly honored, for it is the Passive Intelligence” [III.1 ¶40].

E1277.summary: The pure, indeterminate receptive nature that should reflect the Divine Light unrefracted; identified as the Alchemists' Matter.
E1277.body: Atwood: “And the Passive Nature ought indeed to be a thing of this kind, pure and indeterminate” [III.2 ¶60], reflecting the Divine Light without refraction or mixed images. Identity asserted: “Such was the Matter so often celebrated by the Alchemists” [III.2 ¶60].

E1278.summary: The receptive spirit, spoken of as herself, whose returning faith and desire draw the Soul back into itself at the extreme of tribulation.
E1278.body: Atwood: at the extreme of tribulation, “the returning faith and desire of the Passive Spirit attracts the Soul again into herself” [III.3 ¶10].

E1279.summary: Nature's receptive spirit, enclosed and impure in its ordinary state, made a right recipient by dissolution.
E1279.body: Atwood: in its ordinary state “the passive spirit of nature is included and impure” [I.2 ¶48]; dissolution makes it a right recipient [I.2 ¶48].

E1280.summary: That which the Vital Spirit's fermentation changes; not further defined.
E1280.body: Atwood speaks of “the change that is thereby effected in the Passive Subject” by the Vital Spirit's fermentation [III.1 ¶9]. The text does not define it further.

E1281.summary: Understanding gained in transcendental contemplation of herself, which directs the mode of analysis and supplies most of its means.
E1281.body: Atwood: “the Passive Understanding gotten in transcendental contemplation of herself” directs the mode of analysis and provides most of its means [III.1 ¶40]. The passage does not explicitly identify it with the Passive Intelligence discussed alongside it.

E1282.summary: The first source of life and the last initiation, goal of every step of ascent, whose rebirth in the Free Ether ends the rites.
E1282.body: Atwood: “the paternal is the first source of life, and the last into which the conscience is initiated” [II.4 ¶25]. It is the goal of all steps of ascent, and its rebirth in the Free Ether ends the rites [II.4 ¶25].

E1283.summary: In the Chaldaic Oracle, the source from which intellectual notions crop the Flower of Life.
E1283.body: Voice: the Chaldaic Oracle (quoted): “Intellectual notions from the Paternal Fountain cropping the Flower of Life” [II.4 ¶32]. Not further explained.

E1284.summary: In the Appendix, the fundamental life sought by the light; related expressions Paternal ens and Paternal Spirit dwell in liberty in Elysium.
E1284.body: Appendix only (Table Talk, later layer). Atwood speaks of “seeking the Paternal Life, the fundamental life” [APP ¶167]. Related expressions name what dwells there: “where the Paternal ens resides in liberty” [APP ¶168] and “to Elysium, where the Paternal Spirit lives” [APP ¶171]; the text does not state in so many words that these are the same as the Paternal Life.

E1285.summary: The soul's original, more central light, antecedent to the Maternal intelligence; identified with the generative light.
E1285.body: Atwood calls it “the yet more central, antecedent Paternal, light of life”, into which the Maternal intelligence leads [III.1 ¶34]. In the Appendix (Table Talk, later layer) it is the soul's original light, obscured by the vaporous vehicle to bring it into sense, and identified: “the pure paternal light of life --- the generative light” [APP ¶121].
